lead: Mixed reality has no keyboard or mouse. You look, pinch, speak, or press a controller button, and the system must guess your intent and answer in a frame or two. This chapter covers the input set, the four interaction tasks, near and far interaction, gaze-and-commit, gesture design, feedback, surface anchoring, navigation and wayfinding. It ends with the measures used to test an interaction. The same loop appears in a shop-floor repair guide, a surgical rehearsal, and a phone AR game.
prereq: You need: Unit 5 for manipulation, travel, wayfinding and system control; Unit 2 for gesture interfaces and hand tracking; and 6.2 for the display.

blocks.text: A 6-DoF controller reports six numbers per frame: position (x, y, z) and orientation (yaw, pitch, roll). A hand tracker reports joint poses, the position and orientation of each finger joint. A pinch is thumb tip meeting index tip; a grab is a closed hand around a virtual object. Eye gaze gives a ray from the eye. Voice gives a command word. A mapped table or wall can act as a control surface: tap it, and a menu anchors there.

items: Selection: choose an object or command. Aim with a hand ray or gaze; confirm.
Manipulation: move, rotate, or scale an object. Grab it, then move the hand.
Travel: move the viewpoint. This is navigation, not object motion.
System control: menus, mode changes, save, undo.

blocks.text: Near interaction is within arm's reach: touch or grab a hologram. It is precise and uses real surfaces. Far interaction uses a ray from the hand or eye to a distant object. It gives reach, but aiming error grows with distance and hand tremor. Use near for assembly and far for room-scale menus.

The four tasks are separate. In a repair task, selection picks the bolt, manipulation turns it, travel moves you to the panel, and system control opens the checklist. A single pinch may do selection and manipulation, so the system must know the current mode.

Gaze alone is noisy: a glance may be accidental. In gaze-and-commit the user looks to aim, then pinches or says 'select' to fire. The commit removes ambiguity. Dwell is a fallback: hold gaze for about 800 ms. Too short causes false clicks; too long feels slow.

items: Use few gestures, perhaps four to six.
Make them easy to hold and visually distinct; pinch and grab must not blur.
Avoid long holds; they tire the hand and raise recognition errors.
Keep the elbow low and the gestures short; raised-arm holds cause gorilla arm.

blocks.text: Every action needs feedback: a hover highlight before selection, a sound on commit, a haptic pulse on the controller, and a visible state change. At 60 frames/s one frame is 16.7 ms. A confirmation after several frames feels like a miss.
To place content, cast a ray to a mapped plane, show a preview, then anchor. The anchor stores a pose relative to the real surface, so the hologram stays put when the user walks. Add an undo gesture.

Multimodal commands pair two channels, such as gaze plus voice or pinch plus voice. Two channels cut errors because a false gaze or a misheard word alone is rejected. The chance that both fail in the same way is smaller. Keep the pair natural and fast.

Navigation, or travel, moves the viewpoint. Walking is natural but limited by the room. Teleport points to a floor spot and jumps, which avoids sickness. World-in-miniature lets the user move a small avatar on a model. Portals are doorways to another space. Floor arrows guide steps without a jump.

Wayfinding is knowing where to go, separate from travel. Support it with landmarks, a route preview, a minimap, and turn-by-turn arrows on the floor. In a hospital AR guide, a line on the floor plus a minimap beats a compass.

Measure task time in seconds, error rate in percent, selection accuracy in percent, comfort rating, and workload score from a standard questionnaire such as NASA-TLX. Selection accuracy is correct selections divided by attempts. Compare near against far, or gaze against controller, with enough trials. Report the mean and the spread.

figure.caption: The loop runs for every action. Notice the confidence check between recognition and response, and the feedback path back to the user.

spec.title: MR interaction loop
spec.aria: Interaction loop for mixed reality: the user's gaze, pinch or voice is sensed, recognised, given a confidence, turned into a system response, and answered with visual, audio or haptic feedback.

examples.question: A gesture recogniser is tested with two gestures, pinch and grab, 50 trials each. Of the 50 pinch trials, 46 are called pinch, 3 are called grab and 1 is missed. Of the 50 grab trials, 45 are called grab, 4 are called pinch and 1 is missed. Find accuracy, and the precision and recall of pinch. State what each mistake means for the user.
steps: 2. Correct calls = 46 pinch correct + 45 grab correct = 91. The errors are 3 pinch-to-grab, 1 missed pinch, 4 grab-to-pinch and 1 missed grab, for 9 errors.
4. Pinch precision = true pinch / all called pinch = 46/(46 + 4) × 100 = 92%.
5. Pinch recall = true pinch / all pinch trials = 46/50 × 100 = 92%.

6. The 4 grab trials called pinch cost precision; the 1 missed pinch plus 3 pinch trials called grab cost recall. Both give a wrong action, so raise the pinch confidence threshold and add a hover highlight before commit.
examples.answer: Accuracy is 91%, pinch precision is 92%, and pinch recall is 92%.
examples.check:
pinch_true = 46
grab_true = 45
grab_as_pinch = 4
total = 100
accuracy = (pinch_true + grab_true) / total * 100
precision = pinch_true / (pinch_true + grab_as_pinch) * 100
recall = pinch_true / 50 * 100
print(accuracy)
print(precision)
print(recall)

traps: Travel moves the viewpoint, wayfinding is knowing where to go, manipulation moves the object. Do not mix them.
Treating gaze as a click: a glance is noisy; use commit or dwell with a visible hover.
Designing many similar gestures or long raised-arm holds; recognisers confuse them and the arm tires (gorilla arm).
Copying fixed desktop menus into a head-worn view; place spatial menus within reach or on mapped surfaces.
Late feedback: a confirmation after a few frames feels like a miss; keep it within one or two frames.

quiz.q: Name the four interaction tasks in MR.
quiz.a: Selection, manipulation, travel or navigation, and system control.

quiz.q: Why does gaze-and-commit need a separate commit?
quiz.a: Gaze alone is noisy and can trigger accidental actions. A pinch, voice word or dwell confirms intent.

quiz.q: A recogniser has 80 pinch trials: 72 pinch, 5 grab, 3 missed. It has 80 grab trials: 76 grab, 4 pinch. Find accuracy, pinch precision and pinch recall.
A user must select a small valve across a 2 m room. Compare near and far interaction.
quiz.a: Far interaction with a hand ray is quick but has aiming error at 2 m. Near interaction requires walking closer but is more precise. Use a far ray with hover and commit, or teleport near for fine work.

quiz.q: List four feedback channels for an MR action.
quiz.a: Hover highlight, sound, haptic pulse, and a visible state change.

quiz.q: Why is gorilla arm a design constraint?
quiz.a: Holding the arm raised tires the shoulder quickly. Use short, low gestures and avoid long holds.

quiz.q: Why can gaze plus voice cut selection errors?
quiz.a: The two channels have largely independent errors. A false gaze or a misheard word alone is rejected, so the chance that both fail in the same way is smaller.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry is moving to hand tracking plus eye tracking in lightweight glasses; the hard parts are power, latency, and false positives. Researchers test gesture sets with Fitts'-law style tasks and report throughput in bits per second. Search for 'gaze and commit', 'hand tracking joint poses', 'MR interaction evaluation', and 'NASA-TLX'. Newer headsets build scene meshes from outward cameras, so surface anchoring is becoming a software primitive.
